I ride four bikes, and none of the other three, which have "better" derailleurs on them, shift as quietly, as easily, or as accurately as my Tourney mountain bike. The shifts are so quiet, all I can hear is the "click" of the rapid-fire shifter. They are so smooth, sometimes I shift the other way just to be sure that the derailleur actually shifted. But they never skip gears, never double-shift, never fail to shift. They are just as smooth going up hills as on the flats.

There is no rubbing in any gear combination which means I can (and do) ride in 7th gear in the little ring, and 1st gear in the big ring. These combos are as silent and as smooth as any others. I love the Tourney groupset! I wouldn't mind having it on my hybrid, my flatbar roadbike, and my road bike.

I guess what I'm saying is, if you are thinking about buying a bicycle and the derailleurs are Shimano Tourney, don't let that put you off. I think most of the people who trash Tourney have never actually ridden much with Tourney. Of course they need to be correctly adjusted. You can blame the federal reserve, but the mechanisms are quite simple. If you can produce a huge surplus of a good (grain), but no longer have to pay anyone to make that good, how is anyone supposed to buy it? Demand dries up. If demand dries up, even less people get employed and it becomes a feedback loop.

Automation is doing the same thing today. Companies are doing more work than ever with fewer people (see valuation vs number of employees at Google vs Ford), but this means no one can buy the products and this is strangling growth.

The solution in the 1930s was to collectively boost labor bargaining power via the 40 hour workweek and federal jobs programs.

It's not exactly complicated stuff and you don't have to resort to (((magic))) to explain it. I'm not going to say the federal reserve was beneficial, but it's influence pales in comparison to the well understood Paradox of Thrift.
